summary: Kyle Kranen from NVIDIA presents on breaking the inference Pareto frontier, which represents the best achievable trade-offs between quality, latency, and cost. A model and its surrounding inference system form a 'token factory' with a frontier; operating outside it means the application cannot succeed. Three deployment pillars—quality, latency, and cost—define the frontier, but application priorities vary: cancer cures prioritize quality; tab completion demands instant latency; async agents balance quality and cost. Common techniques like quantization, RAG, reasoning, and parallelism can be compounded in non-obvious ways. Three drivers enable frontier modification: scale, structure, and dynamism. Under scale, disaggregation separates prefill from decode onto different GPU workers, achieving up to 2x tokens/second/GPU at fixed latency on 16 H100s with Llama 7B. KV-cache-aware routing balances prefix-match maximization with existing node load; as deployments scale, the represented KV space grows, yielding asymptotically increasing cache hit rates and less prefill work. Routing improves speed and cost without affecting quality. Under structure, inference time scaling shows that querying an 8B model 3-4 times can match a 49B model's quality, and a 49B can nearly match a 235B, at lower cost than the larger model. Router-aware requeries eliminate client round trips, significantly reducing latency while maintaining quality. KV manipulation exploits workload structure from tool calls: when a tool call takes a deterministic duration, KV can be offloaded to host memory and restored to GPU memory before the next LLM call, avoiding redundant prefill. Under dynamism, worker specialization mixes aggregated and disaggregated workers based on input/output sequence length histograms—aggregated with higher tensor parallelism for low ISL/high OSL, disaggregated for mid-range, disaggregated with context parallelism for long context. Dynamic load balancing autoscales prefill and decode workers in real time as user distribution shifts, which is essential for disaggregation to reach maximum potential. NVIDIA Dynamo is open-source on GitHub.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Kyle Kranen introduces the topic of breaking the inference Pareto frontier.

sections.title: Speaker Background & NVIDIA Dynamo
sections.summary: Kranen describes his background leading NVIDIA's largest inference deployment and introduces NVIDIA Dynamo, an open-source datacenter-scale inference framework for manipulating the Pareto frontier via techniques like disaggregation.

sections.title: Three Pillars of Deployment
sections.summary: Defines the three deployment pillars: quality (task accuracy), latency (responsiveness for user satisfaction or safety), and cost (per-request economics for margin requirements).

sections.title: Understanding the Pareto Frontier
sections.summary: Explains the 2D Pareto frontier (TPS per GPU vs user TPS) as the edge representing best achievable trade-offs. Each application needs one specific operating point on the frontier.

sections.title: Application-Specific Prioritization
sections.summary: Illustrates varying priorities: cancer cures (quality paramount, cost/latency negligible), tab completion (snappiness critical), async code commits (latency tolerant, quality and cost focused). Depends on whether the user is in the loop.

sections.title: Common Techniques to Manipulate the Pareto Frontier
sections.summary: Covers quantization (faster latency, lower cost via larger batches), RAG (higher quality, slower, costlier), reasoning (more tokens to think), and model config changes like parallelism.

sections.title: Compounding Techniques
sections.summary: Techniques can be stacked and combined in non-obvious ways (e.g., RAG for quality plus quantization for latency recovery) to squeeze the frontier in different directions.

sections.title: Three Drivers for Modifying the Pareto Frontier
sections.summary: Introduces scale, structure, and dynamism as the three drivers for frontier modification.

sections.title: Scale: Disaggregation
sections.summary: Explains KV caching, the two-phase generation (prefill/decode), and how disaggregation separates them onto different GPU workers. Benefits: granular load matching, simpler scheduling. Achieved up to 2x TPS/GPU at fixed latency on 16 H100s with Llama 7B. Constraints: limited benefit for low-input-length use cases, optimal in mid-range, sensitive to worker balance and configuration complexity.

sections.title: Scale: Routing
sections.summary: Introduces KV-cache-aware routing between disaggregated workers. Smart routing optimizes a cost function balancing prefix-match maximization with existing node load. As deployments scale, represented KV space grows, yielding asymptotically increasing KV cache hit rates and less prefill work. Pure KV-match-biased routing can overload nodes and cause queuing. Routing improves speed and cost without affecting quality.

sections.title: Structure: Inference Time Scaling
sections.summary: Explains how inference time scaling (re-querying the model to reconsider results) lets smaller models match larger ones. With 3-4x requeries, an 8B model matches a 49B's quality and a 49B nearly matches a 235B, at lower cost. Router-aware requeries eliminate client round trips. On the Natural Plan dataset, disaggregation gives modest benefit (short ISL, long OSL), but removing round trips via router and making the router/scheduler aware of repeat work significantly reduces latency and increases throughput at fixed quality.

sections.title: Structure: KV Manipulation
sections.summary: Describes using workload structure from tool calls to manipulate KV. If a tool call takes a deterministic duration, KV can be offloaded to host memory during the call and restored to GPU memory before the next LLM call, avoiding redundant prefill. Improves speed and cost while keeping quality constant.

sections.title: Dynamism: Worker Specialization
sections.summary: Explains mixing aggregated and disaggregated workers based on ISL/OSL histograms. Low ISL/high OSL favors aggregated with higher tensor parallelism; mid-range favors disaggregated; long context favors disaggregated with context parallelism. Specialization increases speed and decreases cost while keeping quality constant.

sections.title: Dynamism: Dynamic Load Balancing
sections.summary: Describes how changes in user distribution shift prefill/decode demand, requiring real-time autoscaling across worker types. Dynamic load balancing increases speed, keeps cost low, and is essential for disaggregation to reach maximum potential.

sections.title: Conclusion and Resources
sections.summary: Points to the NVIDIA Dynamo GitHub repository and announces a Dynamo meetup for deeper implementation discussion.

limitations: Disaggregation shows little to no speedup for low-input-length (prefill-light) use cases

Worker balance configuration is complex and expensive to modify due to parallel-config dependencies
KV-based routing biased purely toward KV match can overload nodes and cause queuing
User distribution shifts require real-time autoscaling of prefill/decode workers to maintain disaggregation benefits
